[SECTION] Abstract [PAGE] 1
[PARAGRAPH]
Current explanation techniques towards a transparent Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) mainly focuses on building connections between the human-understandable input features with models' prediction, overlooking an alternative representation of the input, the frequency components decomposition. In this work, we present an analysis of the connection between the distribution of frequency components in the input dataset and the reasoning process the model learns from the data. We further provide quantification analysis about the contribution of different frequency components toward the model's prediction. We show that the vulnerability of the model against tiny distortions is a result of the model is relying on the high-frequency features, the target features of the adversarial (black and white-box) attackers, to make the prediction. We further show that if the model develops stronger association between the low-frequency component with true labels, the model is more robust, which is the explanation of why adversarially trained models are more robust against tiny distortions.

[SECTION] Introduction [PAGE] 1
[PARAGRAPH]
The gap between human's understanding and the logic behind Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are receiving more attention as DNNs show competitive inference power in areas where humans used to be indispensable, e.g. medical diagnosis, auto-piloting, and credit systems. Entrusting users by explaining models' behavior becomes as necessary as promoting the performance. Explanations of deep neural networks tend to provide human-understandable descriptions about models' behaviors. Recent work of explanations focuses on associating importance of input features either to the model's output (e.g. Karpathy et al. (2015), Sundararajan et al. (2017), Selvaraju et al. (2019)) or to the

[PARAGRAPH]

distribution of data with which the model is trained (e.g. Koh & Liang (2017), Yeh et al. (2018), Leino et al. (2018)); Among all behaviors of deep models, the robustness draws increasing attentions due to the security and fairness concerns. Current discussion of models' robustness focuses on the capacity of defending adversarial attacks which aims to fool the deep models with similar input but the change is in-perceptional to humans(Szegedy et al., 2013). Different adversarial attacks, though varying in the adversarial loss and updating rules, have been proved to successfully fool the most of deep models. (Szegedy et al. (2013), Goodfellow et al. (2014), Kurakin et al. (2016), Carlini & Wagner (2017), Papernot et al. (2016)).

[SECTION] Introduction [PAGE] 1
[PARAGRAPH]
Besides the work that aims to generate more robust model against existing attacks (Madry et al. (2017), Shafahi et al. (2019)) or a certifiable robust mechanism(Cohen et al. (2019)), the community starts to explain why the deep model tends to be more vulnerable and tries to understand what is behind the adversarial attacks.(Madry et al., 2017) concludes that a robust model tends to be more complex than the standard trained model and Ilyas et al. (2019) shows that adversarial examples can be treated as an input full of non-robust features, which are poorly correlated to the labels. Models can still have good performance and generalizations by only learning the non-robust features but will become vulnerable against various attacks.

[SECTION] Introduction [PAGE] 1
[PARAGRAPH]
However, the community may overlook another facet of input data - the distribution of frequency components. Treating inputs as signals in R n space, we can decompose them into basis signals of diverse frequencies. While humans may only respond to a specific range of frequencies, DNNs are capable of using information from all frequencies. In this paper, we build the bridge between the model's robustness with the distribution of frequency components in the input set. Our major contributions are:

[SECTION] Introduction [PAGE] 1
[PARAGRAPH]
We prove that when the distortion is measured with glyph[lscript] 1 distance, perturbing high-frequency components causes smaller change compared with the lowfrequency components.

[SECTION] Introduction [PAGE] 1
[PARAGRAPH]
We show that, for many existing adversarial attacks, there are more distortions in the high-frequency components.

[SECTION] Introduction [PAGE] 2
[PARAGRAPH]
We propose, Occluded Frequency, our measurement of the contribution of each frequency component towards the prediction and we further show that robust models are usually less relied on the high-frequency components in the input; therefore, they are more robust.

[SECTION] Background and Related Work [PAGE] 2
[PARAGRAPH]
Besides in the original feature space, several works provide new insights into the CNN behaviors from the aspect in the frequency domain. Wang et al. (2019) shows that unlike human beings, high-frequency components play significant roles in promoting CNN's accuracy. Adopting information from high-frequency components may cause the model to form very different concepts in learning as humans do. By observing adversarial defended models, Wang et al. (2019) concludes that smoothing the CNN kernels helps to enforce the model to use features of low frequencies. While the conclusion remains questionable due to the lack of theoretical proof is discussed, the paper proposes a novel view of attributing the frequencies components to the model's predictions. An alternative view of understanding the importance of frequency components is to observe a model's behavior when specific frequency components are modified. This area is studied known as the frequency components analysis on adversarial examples. Guo et al. (2018) proposes an adversarial attack only targeting the low-frequency components in an image, which shows that the model does utilize the features in the lowfrequency domains for predictions instead of only learning from high-frequency components. Sharma et al. (2019) demonstrated that state-of-the-art defenses are nearly as vulnerable as undefended models under low-frequency perturbations, which implies current defense techniques are only valid against adversarial attack in the high-frequency domain. On the other side, (Rahaman et al., 2018) shows that ReLU networks tend to learn low-frequency featuers first and then pick up the high-frequency components later.

[SECTION] Notation and Preliminary [PAGE] 2
[PARAGRAPH]
We first introduce the notation we are going to use in the rest of the paper.

[SECTION] Notation and Preliminary [PAGE] 2
[PARAGRAPH]
Notation A deep neural network y = arg max c f c ( x ) that takes an input x ∈ R d and outputs a prediction class y . For simplicity, we omit the bold font and denote the input as x . We denote the glyph[lscript] p norm as || · || p . The Discrete Fourier Transform of x is denoted as X = F ( x ) (discussion to follow).

[SECTION] Notation and Preliminary [PAGE] 2
[PARAGRAPH]
Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) By convolution with a series of complex-valued exponential functions, DFT transforms a finite signal into the a complex-valued function of frequency. DFT is widely used in signal processing to analyze the frequency components for signals and human are more perceptional to the low frequency components in the signal, e.g. the content of image, while less perceptional to the high-frequency patterns, e.g. noise and small perturbations. Computing DFT requires dealing with complex function and we avoid this by introducing Discrete Cosine Transform in the real implementation but the analysis is still under DFT (Bracewell & Newbold, 1986).

[SECTION] Notation and Preliminary [PAGE] 2
[PARAGRAPH]
Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) DCT is similar to the discrete Fourier transform: it transforms a signal or image from the spatial domain to the frequency domain, but only maintaining the real part. The difference is the basis function: DFT uses complex exponential functions while the DCT uses real-valued cosine functions (Narasimha & Peterson, 1978). In the analysis part, we use DFT to demonstrate the motivations and methods while for the experiments we will replace DFT with DCT due to the imaginary components of DCT will bring extra computational complexity.

[SECTION] Adversarial Attacks [PAGE] 2
[PARAGRAPH]
An adversarial attack tries to find a neighbor of an input x whose prediction is different from x but the change is in-perceptional to humans, causing failure in the reasoning. We introduce a few representative adversarial attack algorithms and methods. We discuss the three white-box attacks to be evaluated in this paper. Goodfellow et al. (2014) proposes FGSM attack , a heuristic searching for the adversarial examples following the sign of adversarial directions with a baby step at each time. It is usually done in the glyph[lscript] ∞ space by clipping the value outside the userdefined pixel range. Unlike FGSM, PGD (Madry et al., 2017) projects the adversarial samples learned from each iteration into the glyph[lscript] p ball of the original input, therefore, the adversarial perturbation size is than the maximum allowed perturbation. CW attack Carlini & Wagner (2017) reformalizes the adversarial loss to ensure that the solution to the optimization is close to the global optimal. They also solve the perturbation in the tanh space to yield the smoothness of the gradient signal. Besides the white-box attacks, we are also interested in the black-box attack and we include SimBA (Guo et al., 2019) in this paper. Under untargeted attack mode, SimBA tries to add a random perturbation on the input image at each step, and accept the perturbation if it decreases prediction certainty on the correct label.

[SECTION] Contribution of Frequency Components [PAGE] 4
[FIGURE]
Caption: Figure 1. Average Attribution scores for each frequency components on each subset of CIFAR-10. We compute the attribution scores on three ResNet models: natural training (blue), Madry's training with glyph[epsilon1] = 0 . 25 in glyph[lscript] 2 space (orange) and Madry's training with glyph[epsilon1] = 0 . 5 in glyph[lscript] 2 space (green). Robust models tend to shift the high attribution scores from the high frequency range to the low frequency range, compared to the naturally trained models. Better viewed in color.
Visual summary: The figure consists of ten subplots arranged in a 2x5 grid, each corresponding to a specific class labeled from "Class 0" to "Class 9." The x-axis of every subplot is labeled "Frequency Basis," with values ranging approximately from 0 to 32, and the y-axis is labeled "Average Frequency Attribution," with values ranging roughly from 0 to 8.

Each subplot displays four line plots representing different conditions or models: "nat" (natural, shown in solid blue), "L2 0.25" (dashed orange), "L2 0.5" (dash-dotted green), and "Linf 8" (dash-dot-dotted red). These lines reflect the average frequency attribution across the frequency basis for each class.

Key trends:
- Across all classes, there is a prominent peak near the lower end of the frequency basis (close to 0), where the attribution reaches its highest value, mostly between 6 and 8, depending on the class and condition.
- After this initial peak, all conditions show a sharp decline, followed by a gradual decrease in average frequency attribution as frequency basis increases.
- The "nat" condition (blue line) consistently exhibits a smoother and more stable attribution across mid to high-frequency ranges compared to the other conditions.
- Regularized conditions ("L2 0.25," "L2 0.5," and "Linf 8") have very similar patterns, often overlapping, with slightly higher peaks near low frequencies compared to "nat." They tend to quickly taper toward zero as frequency increases.

Comparisons and anomalies:
- For Classes 0, 1, and 2, the "nat" condition shows relatively higher attributions at mid to high frequencies (around 10-25 frequency basis) than the regularized conditions.
- An anomaly can be observed in Class 0 and Class 5, where the "nat" condition exhibits a small secondary peak or plateau around frequency basis 15-25, which is less pronounced or absent in the other conditions.
- Classes 3 through 9 display very tight overlap between the "L2" and "Linf" regularized conditions, indicating similar effects of these regularizations on frequency attribution.

Main takeaway:
The figure demonstrates that frequency attribution is dominated by low-frequency components across all classes and conditions. Regularization with L2 or L∞ norms increases the sharpness of the primary low-frequency peak while diminishing contributions from higher frequencies, compared to the natural (unregularized) condition. This suggests that regularization tends to focus frequency attribution towards lower frequencies, potentially enforcing smoother or less complex representations in the frequency domain across all classes.

One of the attribution methods is Occlusion (Zeiler & Fergus, 2013) that ablates a subset of features in the input and assigns the importance score with the change of output compared to the original input. Ablation is usually performed by replacing the features with random noise or a baseline feature, e.g. zeros. We adapt the concept of Occlusion into the frequency domain so that the attribution score of each frequency component is computed by the change of the output of the model. Formally, we propose Occluded Frequency as an attribution method for the spectrum of input.

[SECTION] Contribution of Frequency Components [PAGE] 4
[PARAGRAPH]

Ablation with DCT To perform OF attribution on images with DCT, the masking is performed from the top left corner to the right bottom following the direction of increasing frequencies. All components with the same frequencies are ablated at the same time.

[SECTION] Contribution of Frequency Components [PAGE] 4
[PARAGRAPH]
Why Not Use Gradient Another intuitive choise is to use the gradient-based attribution methods (Simonyan et al., 2013; Sundararajan et al., 2017; Shrikumar et al., 2017) to find the feature importance. However, gradient-based methods are shown to be non-robust and can cause contradictory results for tiny perturbations (Ghorbani et al., 2017). We find the ablation-based attributions are more consistent empirically, therefore, the result is more trustworth.

Caption: Figure 2. RCT maps for different adversarial attacks on 200 images from CIFAR-10. The upper left corner and the lower right corner represent the lowest and highest frequency components in the DCT space, respectively. Visual summary: The figure consists of four heatmaps arranged in a 2x2 grid, each representing results from a different untargeted attack method: (a) PGD Attack, (b) CW Attack, (c) FGSM attack, and (d) SimBA. Each heatmap has x- and y-axes ranging from 0 to 32 with unit markings but no specific unit labels; the axes likely correspond to discrete feature or pixel indices.

The color scale for each heatmap ranges from 0 to 1, with the colorbar displayed on the right side of each plot. The color gradient moves from light yellow (representing values near 0) to dark red (values near 1), indicating some form of intensity or magnitude related to the attack's effect on each coordinate pair.

Key observations:
- Each heatmap shows sparse but distinct dark red spots, signifying locations with the highest measured values (close to 1).
- In (a) PGD Attack and (c) FGSM attack, the high-intensity spots tend to cluster near the lower left quadrant around positions roughly (4,17) and (22,28).
- In (b) CW attack and (d) SimBA, the high-intensity areas shift, with (b) having a prominent spot near (23,28) and (d) showing its peak near coordinates around (6,5), more towards the upper left.
- The majority of the heatmaps exhibit light yellow coloration elsewhere, indicating low intensity or effect over most coordinates.

The main takeaway from this figure is that each untargeted adversarial attack method produces unique spatial patterns of influence or perturbation intensity across the examined coordinate grid. While PGD and FGSM show similar high-value spots, CW and SimBA attacks highlight different regions of peak activity, reflecting variations in their attack strategies or effectiveness distribution profiles.

Visual summary: The figure presents a detailed visual analysis of an image of a truck through discrete cosine transform (DCT) and subsequent frequency attribution.

Top Row (left to right):
- The first panel shows the "Input Image," a pixelated, colored 32x32 image of a truck with visible gridlines on x and y axes ranging from 0 to 32, indicating pixel coordinates.
- The second panel displays the "DCT transformation," a heatmap of the same 32x32 dimensions showing the frequency coefficients after applying the DCT. The top-left corner frequencies exhibit stronger, higher magnitude values represented by brighter colors (yellow-orange), corresponding to low-frequency components.
- The third panel is a bar graph titled "Frequency Attribution," with x-axis labeled in discrete integers 0 to 32 (presumably frequency component indices) and the y-axis showing attribution values roughly from -0.5 to 1.5. This plot reflects how each frequency component contributes to reconstructing or analyzing the image.

Middle Row (left to right):
- The panels labeled "k=1," "k=2," and "k=3" show reconstructions of the image using the top 1, 2, and 3 frequency components, respectively. The "k=1" image is mostly dark with faint shapes, indicating very minimal reconstruction. "k=2" improves visibility, revealing more truck details but still blurred. "k=3" shows further improved clarity but remains coarse.

Bottom Row (left to right):
- These panels display reconstructions based on specific higher-frequency components attributed as top contributors:
   - "k=12 (top1)" shows a relatively distinct and sharper image compared to earlier panels, notably clearer in truck features.
   - "k=23 (top2)" and "k=15 (top3)" also present reasonably clear reconstructions, each highlighting different image details and texture patterns, reinforcing the importance of these frequency components.

Main takeaway:
The figure demonstrates that a sparse selection of DCT frequency components, particularly those with higher attribution values, can effectively approximate the original image. The low-frequency components carry basic shape and color information, while selected mid- to high-frequency components contribute critical details for a clearer reconstruction, highlighting the role of frequency attribution in image compression and reconstruction tasks.

[SECTION] Conclusion [PAGE] 6
[PARAGRAPH]
In this paper, We first show a lower bound of the perturbation applied to the image is related to the lowest frequency components, the most perceptional frequency components to human. We then verify that white-box and black-box attackers mainly focus on the high-frequency components in the clean images. We further propose Occluded Frequency as an attribution method to quantify the contribution of different frequency components in the input. Based on the empirical results on the entire dataset, we provide a frequencybased explanation to answer why standard models are not robust: low-frequency features are more robust than the high-frequency features in the input space; therefore robust models are developed to be strongly related to the lowfrequency features while standard models rely more on the high-frequency components to make the prediction.
